      MCP Docs
      MCP Inspector

      MCP Inspector

      Source: MCP d998c804

      Start with one question and one observable result

      Use the Web client when you need to inspect individual requests or understand a server’s capabilities interactively. Use the CLI when the result must be checked by a script, and the TUI when you want an interactive session without a browser. These are different clients for the same debugging task; starting all three does not provide three independent proofs that your server works.

      Keep the first check narrow: discover a known server, list its tools, then call one harmless tool with valid arguments. Listing tools proves discovery, not successful execution. If the call fails, retain the method, transport, protocol era, and error category before changing configuration. Use synthetic inputs rather than production data.

      ObservationCheck next
      The Web UI opens, but no server is connectedInspect the target command or remote URL and transport; UI startup is not server startup
      Tools are listed, but a call failsCheck that tool’s input schema, required arguments, permissions, and returned error
      An expected feature or tab is absentCompare the selected protocol era and server capabilities before reinstalling
      An unattended CLI command waits for loginUse the documented stored-auth-only workflow for automation and provision credentials separately
      A local check succeeds but a remote check failsCheck routing, authorization, and the actual remotely reachable address before changing business logic

      Read the CLI recipes for machine assertions, protocol eras for legacy/modern differences, and security before sharing a listener. This guide is tied to the attributed documentation revision; it does not claim that whichever package npx resolves today was tested by this site.

      The MCP Inspector is the reference developer tool for testing and debugging MCP servers. It ships as a single package, @modelcontextprotocol/inspector, providing three clients behind one binary:

      ClientInvocationWhat it’s for
      Webnpx @modelcontextprotocol/inspectorA full graphical inspector in the browser. The default, and the richest surface.
      CLInpx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector --cliA scriptable, machine-readable client for CI, shell pipelines, and coding agents.
      TUInpx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector --tuiAn interactive terminal UI, for when a browser isn’t available or wanted.

      All three are built on the same shared core, so a connection behaves identically across them: the same transports, the same configuration files, the same OAuth state on disk, and the same protocol-era negotiation (legacy vs. modern 2026-07-28).

      The package also installs mcpdo, an experimental connection client that connects to a server once and keeps it open across many commands, on the same core.

      Quickstart

      The Inspector requires Node 22.19.0 or newer and runs directly through npx. No installation is required:

      Web 

      # Launch the web UI and connect to a local stdio server
npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector node path/to/server/index.js

# Or launch with no target and add servers from the UI
npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector

      The command prints a URL carrying a per-launch API token and opens it in your browser (set MCP_AUTO_OPEN_ENABLED=false to stop it opening). See Web client.

      CLI 

      # List a server's tools and exit
npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector --cli node path/to/server/index.js --method tools/list

# Call a tool and pipe the result into jq
npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector --cli https://api.example.com/mcp --transport http \
  --method tools/call --tool-name get_weather --tool-arg city=Boston --format json | jq .result

      See CLI client.

      TUI 

      npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector --tui node path/to/server/index.js

      See TUI client.

      Inspecting published servers

      Pass the command that launches the server as the Inspector’s arguments, or point it at a remote server with --server-url:

      npm package 

      npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/inspector npx @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem ~/Desktop

      PyPI package 

      npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector uvx mcp-server-git --repository ~/code/mcp/servers.git

      Remote HTTP server 

      npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector --server-url https://api.example.com/mcp --transport http

      Always read a server’s own README first, since every server requires different commands and arguments.

      The Inspector stores secrets (OAuth tokens, OAuth client secrets, and stdio env: values) in the OS keychain when one is available. On a machine with no keychain (Linux without libsecret or a Secret Service, headless and SSH sessions, Termux, and containers with a mounted volume) they are saved to ~/.mcp-inspector/secrets.json instead, unencrypted unless you supply a key. See Where secrets are stored for how to get a keychain back, encrypt the file, or keep secrets in memory only.

      Launcher flags vs. client flags

      mcp-inspector, the binary that npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector runs, is a thin launcher. It owns only two things:

      1. The mode flag: --web (default), --cli, or --tui. At most one; passing two errors with Specify at most one of --web, --cli, or --tui.
      2. -h / --help.

      Everything else (--catalog, --config, --server-url, --transport, --method, the OAuth flags) is defined by the client, not the launcher, and the clients do not all define the same set. The Configuration and flags page is organized that way, by owner.

      Mode flags are recognized only at the front of the command line: the first token that isn’t --web / --cli / --tui ends launcher parsing, and everything after it is forwarded to the client unchanged. That’s what lets a literal --cli appear later as one of your server’s own arguments:

      mcp-inspector --cli node server.js --cli   # mode is CLI; the trailing --cli goes to server.js
      --help behaves differently with and without a mode flag. Without one, -h/--help anywhere on the command line (even after a server command) prints the launcher’s help and exits. With a mode flag it is forwarded, so mcp-inspector --cli --help prints the CLI’s full flag reference instead.
